Match
List I (Acts of Colonial Government of India) with

List I (Acts of Colonial Government of India)
A. Charter Act, 1813
B. Regulating Act
C. Act of 1858
D. Pitt's India Act
List II (Provisions)
1. Set up a Board of Control in Britain to fully regulate the East India Company's affairs in India

Codes:
x: The Charter Act 1813 ended the East India Company's trade monopoly in India, except for trade in tea and trade with China. The Regulating Act of 1773 required the Company's directors to submit all important correspondence and documents related to Indian administration to the British government. The Government of India Act 1858 transferred the power of governing India from the East India Company to the British Crown. The Pitt's India Act 1784 established a Board of Control in Britain to supervise and regulate the Company's affairs in India.

Lord Macaulay was the first Law Member of the Governor-General's Council. He influenced the government's educational policy for many years. However, it did not provide for an Indian to be appointed as that Law Member.

s: Under the Charter Act of 1793, to what were the salaries of the Board of Control charged?
x: The Charter Act of 1793 charged the Board of Control's salaries to Indian revenues and increased the Governor-General's control over Bombay and Madras.

s: What did the Charter Act of 1833, the final step towards centralisation, make the East India Company?
o: A trading body with its monopoly restored
A Crown department under the India Office
x: The 1833 Act ended the Company's commercial functions and made it purely administrative, while centralising legislation in the Governor-General-in-Council.

s: How many legislative members did the Charter Act of 1853 add to the Governor-General's Council?
x: The 1853 Act added six legislative members, separating legislative from executive functions of the Council.

s: Under the Charter Act of 1853, how were the Company's territories held?
o: For a fixed period of twenty years only
As independent territories under the Governor-General
As permanent private property of the Court of Directors
In trust for the Crown until Parliament otherwise provided
x: The Act declared that the territories were held in trust for Her Majesty until Parliament otherwise provided.

s: The Law Commission headed by Macaulay, regarded as the origin of the present Law Ministry, was set up under which Act?
x: The Charter Act of 1833 (Saint Helena Act) created a Law Commission under Macaulay, the origin of the Law Ministry. s: By the Act of which year was the Governor-General's power to override his Council first given to Lord Cornwallis?
x: The Act of 1786 gave the override power to Cornwallis; the Charter Act of 1793 extended it to all future Governors-General and Presidency Governors.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Indians' share in administration?

The Charter Act of 1853 introduced open competition for the civil services.
The Macaulay Committee (1854) was set up to give effect to open competition.
The Charter Act of 1833 put open competition into actual operation.
x: The 1833 Act only attempted open competition, which was not implemented; open competition came with the 1853 Act.

s: Which one of the following was the last Charter Act enacted by the British Parliament for the East India Company?
x: The Charter Act of 1853 was the last Charter Act. The Government of India Act, 1858 subsequently transferred the governance of India from the East India Company to the Crown.

s: Which of the following about the Charter Act, 1813 is INCORRECT?
o: It permitted Christian missionaries to work in India.
It completely abolished the Company's trade monopoly in India.
It retained the Company's monopoly over the tea and China trade.
It provided an annual grant of ₹1 lakh for education.
x: The 1813 Act ended the Company's monopoly only partly, keeping the tea and China trade; complete abolition came in 1833.

s: Which Act introduced 'Dual Control'?
x: Pitt's India Act, 1784 introduced Dual Control; the Regulating Act set up the Supreme Court at Calcutta.

s: Which Act completely abolished the Company's trade monopoly in India?
x: The Charter Act, 1833 ended the Company's trade monopoly completely and made it a purely administrative body. The 1813 Act ended it only partly, keeping tea and China trade.

s: Which British Act created the office of Governor-General of India and added a Law Member to the Governor-General’s Council?
x: The Charter Act, 1833 created the office of Governor-General of India and added a Law Member (Macaulay) to the Council. The 1853 Act separated legislative and executive functions.

s: Which Act provided an annual grant of Rs 1 lakh for education in India?
x: The Charter Act of 1813 provided the annual education grant of Rs 1 lakh.

s: By how many years did the Charter Act of 1793 extend the Company's trade monopoly?
x: The Charter Act of 1793 extended the monopoly by 20 years.

s: Which Charter Act allowed Christian missionaries to come to India?
x: The Charter Act of 1813 allowed Christian missionaries, after efforts by Charles Grant and Wilberforce.

s: Which Act separated the legislative and executive functions of the Governor-General's council?
x: The Charter Act of 1853 separated the council's legislative and executive functions and added 6 legislative members.

s: Which body worked out the open competition for the civil services put into operation by the 1853 Act?
x: The 1853 Act put open competition into operation, and the Macaulay Committee of 1854 worked it out.

s: Which Section of the Charter Act, 1833 said no Indian would be debarred from office by religion, birth, descent or colour?
x: Section 87 of the 1833 Act laid this down, though open competition was only attempted then.

s: The Charter Act of 1813 ended the Company's trade monopoly except in which of the following?
x: The 1813 Act did not end the monopoly completely: tea and the China trade remained exceptions. It also permitted missionaries to enter India.

s: Who was the first Law Member of the Governor-General's Council?
x: Macaulay became the first Law Member under the 1833 Act, not Impey; S.P. Sinha was the first Indian Law Member (1909).

s: Who was the last Governor-General of Bengal and the first Governor-General of India?
x: Under the Charter Act of 1833, William Bentinck, the last Governor-General of Bengal, became the first Governor-General of India.

s: Which Charter Act first asserted the sovereignty of the British Crown over the Company's territories in India?
x: The Charter Act of 1813 asserted Crown sovereignty over the Company's territories, besides ending its monopoly except tea and China trade.

s: In the context of Indian history, the principle of 'Dyarchy (diarchy)' refers to
o: Division of the central legislature into two houses
Introduction of double government i.e., Central and
Having two sets of rulers; one in London and another
Division of the subjects delegated to the provinces
x: Dyarchy is derived from the Greek word 'di-arche', which means double rule. In the context of Indian history, the principle of Dyarchy refers to the division of the provincial subjects into 'reserved' and 'transferred' categories. Comparatively important subjects (reserved subjects) such as police, jail, justice, finance and irrigation were to be administered by the governor and his executive council without being responsible to the legislative council. Subjects of lesser importance (transferred subjects) such as education, agriculture, local self-government, etc., were to be administered by the governor with the aid of ministers responsible to the legislative council.

x: According to the Act of 1919, the system of Chamber of Princes with 120 members was created. The Chamber of Princes was established by King-Emperor George V's Proclamation on 23 December 1919, after the Government of India Act 1919 was given royal assent. The chamber was formed to provide a forum in which the rulers of the princely States of India could voice their needs and aspirations to the colonial government. x: The Government of India Act, 1919 introduced diarchy at the provincial level. The provincial governments' subjects were separated into two divisions : reserved subjects and transferred subjects. s: The Indian Legislature was made bicameral for the first time by
o: The Government of India Act of 1919
The Government of India Act of 1935
x: The Government of India Act, 1919, made the Indian Legislature bicameral for the first time. It was to consist of an Upper House named the Council of state and a Lower House named the Legislative Assembly. Council of State was composed of 60 members, of whom maximum 20 members could be official in accordance with section 18 of the Government of India Act, 1919. The lower house was called the Central Legislative Assembly and under section 19 of this Act, it originally provided for 140 members with 100 elected and 40 nominated. It is noteworthy that under the Rules made for the implementation of the 1919 Act, provision was made for 60 members with 33 elected and 27 nominated in the Council of State, while the number of members of the Central Legislative Assembly was increased first to 143 (102 elected & 41 nominated) and then to 145 (104 elected and 41 nominated). It is notable that one member in each house was elected from Berar out of the nominated members. Due to a member from Berar being nominated as the result of an election held in Berar, it has been included in the number of elected members in many mentions.

s: Which Act established the Dyarchy system in the Provinces?

The government of India Act of 1919
x: The Government of India Act of 1919, also known as the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms, was passed by the British Parliament with the objective of gradualy introducing responsible Government in India. It introduced a system of dual government at the provincial level. Subjects were divided into two categories. (1) Reserved subjects: These included important areas like law and order, finance, land revenue, and irrigation. These remained under the direct control of the British Governor and his Executive Council. (2) Transferred subjects: These included less critical areas like education, health, public works, and agriculture. This dual scheme of governance was known as ‘dyarchy’-a term derived from the Greek word diarche, which means double rule. It also introduced, for the first time, bicameralism and direct elections in the country.
